content: It is recommended to utilize a PrEP delivery cascade to guide data collection in upcoming demonstration projects and to evaluate their effectiveness. Employing standardized metrics will enable meaningful comparisons across different PrEP programs. Once real-world data from these projects are available, modeling can be used to assess the impact of targeted interventions at various stages of the PrEP cascade, with the ultimate goal of maximizing public health benefits. A study by Marcus et al. (2013) found no evidence of increased sexual risk behaviors (risk compensation) among participants in the iPrEx trial, which evaluated daily oral PrEP with emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (FTC/TDF) for HIV prevention in men who have sex with men and transgender women. Self-reported sexual risk behaviors decreased overall, though reporting bias may have influenced these findings. Biomarkers of sexual risk were used to further evaluate potential risk compensation. Results showed a reduction in acute HIV infections and syphilis during follow-up, and participants who believed they were receiving FTC/TDF had more sexual partners prior to starting the medication, suggesting that risk behaviors were not a consequence of PrEP use. Another study (2013) examined the effects of prolonged FTC/TDF use on lipid profiles in HIV-negative men participating in the iPrEx trial. Results indicated small but statistically significant reductions in cholesterol levels, particularly at week 24, with a tendency to rebound by week 72. These findings suggest that FTC/TDF may independently influence cholesterol levels, separate from its effects on HIV suppression. A trial conducted in Kenya assessed the safety and adherence to intermittent PrEP regimens among men who have sex with men (MSM) and female sex workers (FSW). Participants were randomized to daily or intermittent FTC/TDF or placebo. Despite these challenges, PrEP acceptability was high across dosing regimens. The study concluded that while adherence to intermittent regimens may be more challenging than daily dosing, intermittent PrEP could still be viable if intracellular drug levels sufficient for HIV prevention can be achieved and adherence barriers are addressed. Research on sexual risk trajectories among HIV-negative MSM in the United States identified distinct patterns of risk behavior over time. Screening for socio-demographic and behavioral factors associated with high-risk periods may facilitate targeted PrEP delivery during these intervals. Ethical considerations surrounding PrEP use include issues of safety, risk behaviors, resistance, stigma, and equitable access. Clinicians and policymakers must weigh these factors when prescribing PrEP to at-risk individuals. Additionally, researchers must address ethical dimensions in future HIV prevention studies, including the inclusion of PrEP in prevention packages and the selection of appropriate control arms. Intermittent PrEP dosing, which may reduce costs and toxicity while improving adherence, requires careful planning of sexual activity. MSM who are older, more educated, and frequent users of sexual networking websites may be more suitable candidates for event-based PrEP. However, adherence to such regimens remains a challenge, and further research is needed to optimize strategies for intermittent PrEP use.
